questions.question: Prepare a note on the Films Division of India. Briefly explain its role and contribution to the growth of documentary filmmaking in India. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html: • The Films Division was established in 1948 under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. It produced documentaries, newsreels and short films for public exhibition. It documented national events, development programmes, history, culture and social issues; informed and educated audiences; supported documentary production expertise; and created an audiovisual record of post-Independence India. It helped institutionalise documentary filmmaking and made it an important tool of public communication.

questions.question: Explain the significance of the preliminary research phase in documentary filmmaking, and identify two common methods a filmmaker uses to gather information before shooting begins / [CO2]
questions.solution_html: • Research establishes factual accuracy, identifies the central issue and story thread, locates people and places, reveals ethical or safety concerns, and informs the budget and schedule. Secondary research includes books, reports, archives, articles and existing films. Primary research includes preliminary interviews, site visits, observation and discussions with experts or community members. Research makes the film focused, credible and feasible.

questions.question: Explain why natural and artificial light sources equally need consideration during setup. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html: • Natural light changes with time, weather and sun direction, affecting exposure and continuity. The crew should assess intensity, direction and colour and plan accordingly. Artificial light gives control over brightness, direction and contrast, fills shadows and can separate a subject from the background. Check white balance, mixed colour temperatures, harsh shadows and safety. Balancing both sources supports clear, natural-looking and consistent footage.

questions.question: Explain the primary purpose of a promotional strategy for a documentary film, and identify two different methods a production crew can use to generate public interest before its release. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html: • A promotional strategy helps a documentary reach its intended audience, communicate relevance and build interest before release. It can support festivals, screenings, partnerships and publicity. Methods include (1) a social-media campaign using trailers, posters, short clips, behind-the-scenes content and hashtags; and (2) media/community outreach through press releases, interviews, previews and partnerships with NGOs, colleges or community groups. Promotion should start in pre-production and continue through release.

questions.question: Explain the role of a release/consent form in documentary production. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html: • A release or consent form records a participant’s informed agreement to be filmed or recorded and to have the contribution edited, exhibited or distributed within the agreed scope. It may identify the participant, permitted use of image and voice, and any conditions. It promotes transparency and helps manage legal and ethical risks. Consent should be voluntary and understandable; a signed form does not remove the filmmaker’s duty to protect privacy and avoid misleading representation.

questions.question: Differentiate between a fictional feature film screenplay and a pre-production documentary script, highlighting how their formats reflect the predictability of their stories. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html: • A fiction screenplay usually plans scenes, dialogue, characters and actions in a controlled narrative. A documentary pre-production script may be a proposal, treatment, outline or shooting script identifying the subject, intended structure, likely sequences, interview areas, locations and visual approach. Real events cannot be fully predicted, so documentary plans remain flexible and change as evidence or events emerge. Fiction generally scripts a planned story; documentary scripting prepares for actuality.

questions.question: Describe why sound design is considered as important as visual editing in a documentary / [CO3]
questions.solution_html: • Sound conveys dialogue, location, mood and realism. Clear speech supports understanding; ambient sound establishes place; music may shape emotion and silence can create emphasis. Sound editing balances levels, reduces distracting noise and maintains continuity. Poor sound can undermine excellent visuals. Sound choices should support the evidence and must not manipulate or misrepresent events.

questions.question: Substantiate the need for checking microphone audio levels during equipment setup with relevant points. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html: • Levels that are too low create weak recordings and amplify noise; levels that are too high clip and distort speech. Test with the actual speaker, monitor meters and headphones, leave headroom for loud sounds, check cables and batteries, and listen for wind, clothing rustle, handling noise, echo and background sound. questions.question: Analyse how interviews and observational footage can create a balanced documentary sequence. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Introduction: Interviews and observational footage are complementary methods. Interviews provide testimony, explanation, memory, expert context and viewpoints; observational footage shows actions, places, interactions and everyday details. Interviews: They explain causes, motives and consequences, introduce context and present different perspectives. Select concise sound bites that advance the story. Interview accounts are subjective, so important claims may need verification. Observational footage: It establishes place, shows processes and adds visual evidence, atmosphere and natural sound. However, images also require context; selective framing can mislead. Combining the methods: Begin with an establishing shot, introduce the issue through an interview, use observational scenes or cutaways to show the relevant context, then return to an interview that deepens or challenges the point. Natural sound can bridge edits and maintain continuity. Ethics: Represent contrasting accounts fairly. Do not use unrelated images to imply a false connection or edit words misleadingly. Verify factual claims where possible and respect participants’ privacy and dignity. Conclusion: Interviews provide voice and interpretation, while observation provides action and context. Carefully combined, they produce an informative, engaging and credible sequence.
  • • Opening (0:00–0:40): Notifications and a person about to forward a sensational post. Voice-over: “One tap can inform, mislead or hurt. What do we check before sharing?”
  • • Problem (0:40–1:50): Short staged examples of a rumour, a hurtful comment and oversharing personal details. Identify misinformation, cyberbullying and privacy risks.
  • • Voices (1:50–3:20): Student interviews and expert advice: how to verify a claim, respond to cyberbullying and protect personal information.
  • • Practical response (3:20–5:30): Pause before forwarding; check source and date; read beyond headlines; ask permission before posting others’ images; use privacy settings; block/report abuse; seek trusted help; balance screen time.
  • • Conclusion: A student checks a source before sharing. Voice-over: “Be connected. Be kind. Be responsible.” Visual and sound plan: Use close-ups, screen inserts, medium shots, observational footage and readable graphics. Hide real usernames and private messages. Use clear dialogue, restrained music and natural sound. Ethics and distribution: Label dramatized scenes, verify claims, protect minors and avoid fear-based exaggeration. Edit for clarity, add captions, check audio, and share through college screenings, educational institutions and social platforms. Conclusion: A flexible script combines evidence, real voices and practical actions, leaving viewers with achievable habits.

questions.question: Explain the key aspects of equipment setup - camera, microphone, and lighting - required before a documentary shoot, with technical detail. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html: • Introduction: Systematic setup improves image and sound quality, reduces technical failure and prepares the crew for unpredictable events. Camera: Check batteries, recording media and storage. Select suitable resolution, codec and frame rate according to delivery requirements. Set shutter speed appropriately and check for flicker. Set white balance and exposure; check focus, lens, framing, stabilisation and tripod security. Record and play back a test clip. Keep spare batteries and media. Microphone and audio: Select a lavalier for interviews, boom/shotgun for directional dialogue, or a separate recorder as needed. Place the microphone close enough for clear speech but out of frame and away from clothing friction. Check cables, batteries, wireless signal and recorder settings. Monitor with headphones, set levels with headroom, and listen for wind, traffic, echo, hum and handling noise. Record room tone. When audio and video use separate devices, plan synchronisation using timecode, a clapper or a clear sync event. Lighting: Assess natural light direction and changes throughout the day. Use available light when appropriate; add key, fill or backlight only as required. Manage mixed colour temperatures, shadows and exposure. Secure stands and cables and follow electrical safety. Integrated checks: Test camera, sound and light together at the location, review a sample, label media, confirm permissions and keep backup equipment available. Conclusion: Professional setup depends on coordinated technical checks, not merely owning equipment. Testing before filming prevents avoidable failures and supports consistent footage.
